title: Advanced SQL
text:
The “Window” Concept

The “Window” is the subset of rows relevant to the current row.
The window is defined by the OVER clause.


Think of a window as a sliding lens. As you move down the rows in your table, the lens moves with you, looking at a specific subset of data to perform its math.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Window Function Syntax
SELECT
1    column_name,
2    FUNCTION(column_name) OVER (
3        PARTITION BY column_to_group_by
4        ORDER BY column_to_sort_by
5    ) AS alias_name
6FROM table_name;

1

Include this original column in the output. Window functions preserve individual rows.

2

Apply a window function, such as SUM() or AVG(). The OVER() clause defines how rows are organized for the calculation.

3

Divide the rows into partitions. The function operates independently within each partition.

4

Define the order of rows within each partition for the calculation. This does not guarantee the display order of the final output.

5

Name the calculated output column.

6

Specify the table containing the data.



The OVER clause is what makes it a window function. Inside it, we use PARTITION BY to define our groups and ORDER BY to define the sequence of the calculation.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
PARTITION BY

Divides the result set into partitions.
The function is applied to each partition separately.
It is like GROUP BY for window functions, but it doesn’t hide the individual rows.


PARTITION BY is how we tell SQL where one group ends and the next begins. For example, if we partition by “Department,” the math starts over for every new department.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Activity 1
Using film, return film_id, title, rating, and length for every film with a nonmissing length. Add rating_avg_length: the average length of films with the same rating.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
ORDER BY in Window Functions

Crucial for:

Running Totals (Cumulative sums).
Rankings.
Moving Averages.

It defines the direction in which the window “slides” (e.g., from oldest to newest).


You almost always use ORDER BY inside your OVER clause. Without it, the computer doesn’t know which row comes “before” or “after” another, making rankings or running totals impossible.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Ranking Functions: The Big Three

ROW_NUMBER(): Assigns a unique, sequential integer to rows (1, 2, 3, 4).
RANK(): Assigns the same rank to ties, but skips the next number (1, 2, 2, 4).
DENSE_RANK(): Assigns the same rank to ties, but does not skip numbers (1, 2, 2, 3).


Not all rankings are created equal. If two people tie for 2nd place, do you want the next person to be 3rd, or 4th? That’s the difference between RANK and DENSE_RANK.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Ranking Comparison Diagram












Row Number: Strictly unique.
Rank: Leaves gaps.
Dense Rank: No gaps.


This diagram helps visualize the “Gap” behavior. Notice how RANK jumps from 1 to 3 because two people tied for 1st.

DENSE_RANK(): rank by film length

What does each ranking do?

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Value Functions: LEAD and LAG

LAG(column): Accesses data from the previous row.
LEAD(column): Accesses data from the following row.
Use Case: Comparing this month’s sales to last month’s sales to calculate growth.


LEAD and LAG are like time machines. They allow you to look back at the past row or ahead to the future row without needing a complex self-join.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Window Frames: The “Moving” Window
Sometimes, you don’t want to look at the entire partition. You only want a subset of it.

ROWS BETWEEN ...
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING: Start from the very first row of the partition.
CURRENT ROW: End at the row you are on.
1 PRECEDING: Look at exactly one row before.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Window Frames Example
Example: 3-Day Moving Average
AVG(price) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

We can even limit the window size. This is how “Moving Averages” are calculated in finance. Instead of looking at all data, we tell SQL to look at only the last 3 rows.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Activity 5
Using payment, first create a CTE containing one row per payment date: payment_day and daily_revenue. Use DATE(payment_date) to remove the time.

Return each observed payment date and its daily revenue.
Add running_revenue: revenue from the first observed date through the current row.
Add moving_avg_3_rows: average daily revenue over the current row and up to two preceding rows.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Solution 1
SELECT film_id, title, rating, length,
       AVG(length) OVER (
1           PARTITION BY rating) AS rating_avg_length
FROM film
2WHERE length IS NOT NULL
3ORDER BY rating, film_id;

1

Compute the average across the entire rating partition. With no window ordering, this average is repeated for every film in that rating.

2

Exclude missing lengths before calculating the window values.

3

Set the displayed order independently of the window calculation.


Interpretation: A positive difference means the film is longer than its rating’s average. Unlike GROUP BY, this window calculation retains each film row.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Solution 2
SELECT film_id, title, rating, length,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY rating
1           ORDER BY length DESC, film_id) AS row_num,
       RANK() OVER (
           PARTITION BY rating
2           ORDER BY length DESC) AS length_rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (
           PARTITION BY rating
3           ORDER BY length DESC) AS dense_length_rank
FROM film
WHERE length IS NOT NULL
4ORDER BY rating, length DESC, film_id;

1

Assign unique sequential numbers within each rating. The identifier gives tied lengths a repeatable order.

2

Give equal lengths equal ranks; leave gaps after ties.

3

Give equal lengths equal ranks without gaps between distinct lengths.

4

Display ties in identifier order without changing their shared ranks.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Solution 3
1SELECT payment_id, payment_date, amount,
2       LAG(amount) OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id
3       ) AS previous_amount
FROM payment
4WHERE customer_id = 1;

1

Select the columns to be displayed.

2

Creates the window function and applies the lag function to obtain the previous amount.

3

Partitions by customer_id and orders by payment_date and payment_id.

4

Restrict the input to customer 1.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Solution 4
1SELECT customer_id, rental_id, rental_date,
2       LEAD(rental_date) OVER (
3           PARTITION BY customer_id
4           ORDER BY rental_date, rental_id
5       ) AS next_rental_date
6FROM rental
7WHERE customer_id IN (1, 2, 3);

1

Display the customer identifier, rental identifier, and rental timestamp.

2

Use LEAD() to retrieve the following row’s rental date within the window.

3

Create a separate partition for each customer so the next rental belongs to the same customer.

4

Order each customer’s rentals chronologically. Use rental_id to break ties when timestamps match. This controls the window calculation, not the final display order.

5

Name the calculated column next_rental_date. Each customer’s final rental returns NULL because no following rental exists.

6

Retrieve records from the rental table.

7

Include only customers 1, 2, and 3. This filter applies before the window function is calculated.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Solution 5
1WITH daily_sales AS (
2    SELECT DATE(payment_date) AS payment_day,
           SUM(amount) AS daily_revenue
    FROM payment
3    GROUP BY DATE(payment_date)
)
4SELECT payment_day, daily_revenue,
       SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (
5           ORDER BY payment_day
6           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS running_revenue,
       AVG(daily_revenue) OVER (
           ORDER BY payment_day
7           ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS moving_avg_3_rows
8FROM daily_sales
9ORDER BY payment_day;

1

Create a common table expression (CTE) named daily_sales to summarize payments before applying window functions.

2

Extract the date from each payment timestamp, removing the time, and name it payment_day.

3

Group payments by date. SUM(amount) calculates total revenue for each date, producing one row per observed payment date.

4

Display each payment date and its daily revenue.

5

Order the daily rows chronologically for the running-total calculation.

6

Include every row from the beginning through the current row. SUM() over this frame calculates cumulative revenue as running_revenue.

7

Include the current row and up to two preceding rows. AVG() calculates their average daily revenue. The first result uses one row, the second uses two, and subsequent results use three. These are observed payment dates, not necessarily consecutive calendar days.

8

Retrieve the daily summaries from the CTE. Both window functions preserve one output row per observed payment date.

9

Display the final results chronologically. The ordering inside OVER() controls calculations but does not guarantee the final display order.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Agenda

Relational Joins

Inner, Left, Right, Full, Cross, and Self Joins

Subqueries

Scalar, Multi-row, and Correlated

Database Views

Virtual tables and Materialized Views



Today we will cover three tools for organizing relational queries: joins, subqueries, and views.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
The Concept of Joins
To combine data from two or more tables, we use a common column (usually a Foreign Key).





graph LR
    A[Table A] --- B{Join Condition}
    C[Table B] --- B
    B --> D[Combined Result Set]

    classDef table fill:#0072B2,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff
    classDef logic fill:#E69F00,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000
    classDef result fill:#009E73,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff

    class A,C table
    class B logic
    class D result







Joins are the heart of relational databases. We look for a “bridge” between tables to pull related information together in a single result set.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text: Inner Join

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Inner Join
Returns records that have matching values in both tables.
SELECT 
    employees.name, 
    departments.dept_name
FROM employees
INNER JOIN departments 
ON employees.dept_id = departments.id;

Only matches are returned.
If an employee has no department, they are excluded.
If a department has no employees, it is excluded.


The Inner Join is the most common join. Think of it as the “intersection” of two sets. If there is no overlap, you get nothing.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text: Left Join

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Left Join
Returns all records from the left table, and the matched records from the right table.
SELECT 
    employees.name, 
    departments.dept_name
FROM employees
LEFT JOIN departments 
ON employees.dept_id = departments.id;

If there is no match, the result is NULL on the right side.
Useful for finding “missing” relationships.


The Left Join is crucial when you want to keep your primary list intact, regardless of whether the second table has matching data.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text: Right Join

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Right Join
Returns all records from the right table, and the matched records from the left table.
SELECT 
    employees.name, 
    departments.dept_name
FROM employees
RIGHT JOIN departments 
ON employees.dept_id = departments.id;

The opposite of a Left Join.
Includes all departments, even those without employees.
Requires SQLite 3.39.0 or later.


While Right Join exists, many developers prefer using Left Join and simply switching the order of the tables to keep their logic reading from left to right.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text: Full Join

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Full Join
Returns all records when there is a match in either the left or right table.
SELECT 
    employees.name, 
    departments.dept_name
FROM employees
FULL OUTER JOIN departments 
ON employees.dept_id = departments.id;

Combines the effect of Left and Right joins.
Provides a complete picture of all data in both tables.
Requires SQLite 3.39.0 or later.


Full Outer Join is used when you want to see everything from both sides, showing where matches exist and where they don’t.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Self Join
A join where a table is joined with itself.
SELECT 
    e1.name AS Employee, 
    e2.name AS Manager
FROM employees AS e1
INNER JOIN employees AS e2 
ON e1.manager_id = e2.id;

Requires table aliasing (e1, e2).
Used for hierarchical data (e.g., Employee -> Manager).


Self joins are essential for organizational charts or any data structure where a row has a relationship with another row in the same table.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Subqueries
A subquery is a query nested inside another query.





graph TD
    Outer[Outer Query / Main Query] -->|Contains| Inner[Inner Query / Subquery]
    Inner -->|Returns Data| Outer

    classDef outer fill:#0072B2,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    classDef inner fill:#E69F00,stroke:#333,color:#000

    class Outer outer
    class Inner inner







Subqueries allow for complex, multi-step data retrieval in a single statement. They can be used in SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and HAVING clauses.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Scalar Subqueries
A subquery that returns exactly one value (one row, one column).
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);

Returns a single value for comparison.
Often used in SELECT or WHERE.


Scalar subqueries are very efficient for comparing individual rows against an aggregate value, like finding people paid more than the average.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Multi-row Subqueries
Subqueries that return a list of values (one column, multiple rows).
SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IN 
  (SELECT id FROM departments WHERE location = 'New York');

Common operators include IN, ANY, ALL, and EXISTS.
Used to filter against a dynamic list.
SQLite supports IN and EXISTS, but not the SQL-standard ANY and ALL operators directly.


Multi-row subqueries are powerful for filtering one table based on a set of criteria found in another table without using a traditional JOIN.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views

Activity: Subqueries

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Views: Definition
A View is a “virtual table” based on the result-set of an SQL statement.

It does not store data itself (unless it is a Materialized View).
It is a stored query.
It acts as a window into your real tables.


Views are not actual tables. They are saved queries that look and behave like tables.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Why use Views?

Security: Hide sensitive columns (like salaries or SSNs) by creating a view that only shows non-sensitive info.
Simplicity: Simplify complex joins into a single “virtual” table.
Consistency: Standardize how specific logic (like “Active Customers”) is calculated across the organization.


Instead of writing a 50-line JOIN query every time, you can write it once, save it as a view, and then just SELECT * FROM my_view.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Creating and Using Views
-- Creating a view
CREATE VIEW active_employee_contact AS
SELECT name, email, phone
FROM employees
WHERE status = 'Active';

-- Using the view
SELECT * FROM active_employee_contact;

You can use SELECT, JOIN, and WHERE on a view just like a table.


Once the view is created, it becomes part of your database schema for all users with permission to access it.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Materialized Views
Unlike standard views, Materialized Views actually store the data physically.

Pros: Extremely fast for heavy calculations or large aggregations.
Cons: The data can become “stale” (outdated) and must be refreshed.
SQLite note: SQLite does not provide native materialized views.

-- Refreshing a materialized view (syntax varies by DB)
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW sales_summary;

Use Materialized Views for reporting/dashboards where the data doesn’t need to be second-by-second real-time, but speed is critical.

text:
Glossary: Query Commands







Command
Purpose




SELECT
Chooses the columns or calculated values to return.


FROM
Identifies the source table, view, or subquery.


WHERE
Filters individual rows before grouping.


GROUP BY
Combines rows that share the same values for aggregate calculations.


HAVING
Filters groups after GROUP BY.


ORDER BY
Sorts the result in ascending or descending order.


LIMIT
Restricts the number of rows returned.


AS
Assigns a temporary alias to a column, table, or calculated value.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Glossary: Joins







Command or term
Purpose




JOIN / INNER JOIN
Returns rows with matching values in both tables.


LEFT JOIN
Returns every row from the left table and matching rows from the right table.


RIGHT JOIN
Returns every row from the right table and matching rows from the left table.


FULL OUTER JOIN
Returns matched rows plus unmatched rows from both tables.


CROSS JOIN
Returns every possible pairing of rows from two tables.


ON
States the condition used to match rows.


Self join
Joins a table to itself by using separate table aliases.


NULL
Represents a missing or unknown value, including an unmatched outer-join value.

title: SQL: Joins, Subqueries, and Views
text:
Glossary: Subqueries and Views







Command or term
Purpose




Subquery
Places one query inside another query.


AVG()
Calculates an arithmetic mean and can supply a scalar subquery value.


COUNT()
Counts rows or non-null values.


SUM()
Adds numeric values.


ROUND()
Rounds a numeric value to a specified number of decimal places.


IN
Tests whether a value occurs in a list returned by a subquery.


EXISTS
Tests whether a subquery returns at least one row.


ANY / ALL
Compare a value with some or every value from a subquery. SQLite does not support these operators directly.


CREATE VIEW
Saves a query as a virtual table.


DROP VIEW
Removes a view definition.


REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
Updates stored materialized-view results in systems that support the command. SQLite does not.

    FROM Track

Subqueries Activity: Solution 2
SELECT Name, UnitPrice
FROM Track
WHERE GenreId IN (
    SELECT GenreId
    FROM Genre
    WHERE Name IN ('Rock', 'Metal')

title: Data Systems
text:
What is a Data System?
A data system is a collection of interconnected components used to collect, store, process, and analyze data.

Input: Raw data (logs, transactions, sensor readings).
Process: Transformation and cleaning.
Storage: Databases or Data Lakes.
Output: Insights, reports, or machine learning models.


Think of a data system like a water treatment plant. You have raw water (input), a filtration system (processing), a reservoir (storage), and tap water for consumption (output).

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Types: The Big Picture
Data is categorized based on how much “organization” it has before it enters a system.

Structured: Highly organized (e.g., Excel, SQL).
Semi-structured: Organized but flexible (e.g., JSON, XML).
Unstructured: No predefined model (e.g., Video, PDF, Audio).


Understanding the format of your data determines what kind of database you need and how much work you have to do to clean it.

title: Data Systems
text:
Structured Data

Tabular (rows and columns).
Highly organized.
Easily searchable.
Examples:

Customer names and addresses.
Transaction amounts and dates.
Inventory counts.



Structured data is the most common form of data handled by traditional businesses. It fits perfectly into spreadsheets and relational databases.

title: Data Systems
text:
Semi-Structured Data

Does not reside in a rigid grid.
Contains tags or markers to separate data elements.
Flexible schema (can change easily).
Examples:

JSON: Used in web APIs.
XML: Used in configuration files.
CSV: Simple comma-separated values.



Semi-structured data is the “middle ground.” It has some hierarchy and markers, but you can add new fields without rebuilding the whole table.

title: Data Systems
Data Systems
text:
Unstructured Data

No internal structure or predefined model.
Makes up the vast majority of data generated today.
Requires specialized tools (AI/ML) to extract meaning.
Examples:

Emails (the text part).
Images and Videos.
Social media posts.



Think of a photo. A computer just sees a bunch of pixels. It doesn’t know it’s a “cat” until an unstructured data processing tool (like an AI model) analyzes it.

title: Data Systems
text:
Relational Databases (RDBMS)
The traditional way of storing structured data.

Core Concept: Data is organized into tables.
Schema: Rigid and predefined (must define columns before inserting data).
Relationships: Tables are linked via “Keys” (Primary and Foreign keys).
Example: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle.


In a relational database, if you want to add a “Phone Number” column, you have to update the entire table structure first. This is called a “schema change.”

title: Data Systems
text:
Relational Properties: ACID
To ensure data integrity, RDBMS follow ACID properties:

Atomicity: “All or nothing” transactions.
Consistency: Data follows all rules (no broken links).
Isolation: Transactions don’t interfere with each other.
Durability: Once saved, it stays saved (even if power fails).


ACID is critical for banking. If you transfer $10, the money must leave your account AND arrive in the other account. It cannot do one without the other.

title: Data Systems
text:
Non-Relational Databases (NoSQL)
Designed for modern, high-scale, and flexible data.

Core Concept: Data is stored as documents, key-value pairs, or graphs.
Schema: Dynamic/Flexible (no predefined structure required).
Scalability: Designed to scale “out” (adding more servers).
Example: MongoDB (Document), Redis (Key-Value), Neo4j (Graph).


NoSQL is the response to the “Big Data” explosion. When you have massive amounts of unstructured or semi-structured data, relational databases can struggle to scale.

Different NoSQL types are specialized for different tasks. A graph database is perfect for a social network where you need to track “friend of a friend” connections.

If your data structure is predictable and consistency is paramount (like finance), go SQL. If your data is changing fast and you need massive scale, go NoSQL.

Activity 2: The Architect’s Dilemma
Scenario: You are building a new social media app like Instagram.

You need to store a “Follower” graph (who follows whom).

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Pipelines
Data doesn’t just sit there; it moves.
Definition: A sequence of data processing steps where a set of data is passed through a series of transformations.
Goal: To move data from a source (where it’s created) to a destination (where it’s used).

A pipeline is like a conveyor belt in a factory. Raw materials go in one end, and finished products come out the other.

title: Data Systems
text:
ETL vs. ELT
The two main ways to move data:


ETL
(Extract, Transform, Load)

Extract from source.
Transform in a staging area (cleaning/filtering).
Load into the target database.


ELT
(Extract, Load, Transform)

Extract from source.
Load directly into the target (Data Lake).
Transform inside the target database using its own power.



ETL was the standard for decades. ELT is becoming more popular because modern cloud warehouses (like Snowflake) are incredibly powerful at processing data once it’s inside.

text:
The Data Pipeline Workflow





%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'primaryColor': '#811331', 'edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff', 'primaryTextColor': '#ffffff', 'lineColor': '#000000' }}}%%

    Ext --> Trans[Transformation]
    Trans --> Load[Loading/Storage]
    Load --> Anal[Analytics/BI]







This shows the journey from the moment a user clicks a button on a website to the moment a CEO sees a chart on their dashboard. A linear flow: Source \(\rightarrow\) Extraction \(\rightarrow\) Transformation \(\rightarrow\) Loading \(\rightarrow\) Analytics.

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Pipeline Components

Source: Where data originates (App logs, DBs, APIs).
Ingestion: The process of pulling data from the source.
Processing/Transformation: Cleaning, aggregating, or renaming fields.
Storage: The final destination (Data Warehouse or Data Lake).
Orchestration: The “brain” that schedules and monitors the steps.


Orchestration is very important. If the “Extraction” step fails, the “Transformation” step shouldn’t try to run on old or broken data.

SQLite date helper: JULIANDAY(later_date) - JULIANDAY(earlier_date) gives elapsed days, potentially including fractions.

title: ICA 6
text:
Probelm 5: Track revenue through time
How are cumulative sales and recent daily sales changing?
Use UnitPrice from "Order Details" for historical sales, rather than the catalog price in Products. Use this supplied CTE to obtain one row per observed order date. Replace the final SELECT with your window calculations.
WITH daily_sales AS (
    SELECT DATE(o.OrderDate) AS order_day,
           SUM(d.UnitPrice * d.Quantity * (1.0 - d.Discount))
               AS daily_revenue
    FROM Orders AS o
    JOIN "Order Details" AS d ON o.OrderID = d.OrderID
    WHERE o.OrderDate IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY DATE(o.OrderDate)
)

Return order_day and daily_revenue.
Add running_revenue using SUM() from the first daily row through the current row. Write the frame explicitly.
Add moving_avg_3_rows using AVG() over the current row and up to two preceding rows.
Round all three monetary columns to two decimals. Display dates ascending.

Why Data Modeling Matters
A data model helps teams agree on:

What data must be stored
How different concepts relate
Which rules protect data quality
How the database supports real questions


Ask students to imagine building a database without a plan. Use examples like duplicate customer records, missing orders, or unclear relationships between students and courses.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Three Levels of Data Models








Level
Main question
Typical output




Conceptual
What does the organization need to track?
Entities and relationships


Logical
How should the data be structured?
Tables, columns, keys, and constraints


Physical
How will the DBMS store and access it?
Data types, indexes, and storage choices




Use this slide to separate planning from implementation. Students often jump straight to tables, but conceptual thinking helps them understand the domain first.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Entity-Relationship Diagrams
An Entity-Relationship diagram, or ER diagram, visually represents:

Entities
Attributes
Relationships
Cardinality rules


Define ER diagrams as a communication tool. They help non-programmers and technical users discuss the structure of a database before creating tables.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Entities
An entity is a thing about which we want to store data.
Examples:

Student
Course
Instructor
Enrollment
Product
Order


Emphasize that entities often become tables in a relational database. Ask students to name entities from a familiar system such as a library, store, or university.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Attributes
An attribute is a fact or property stored about an entity.
For a Student entity, attributes might include:

student_id
first_name
last_name
email
major


Point out that attributes often become columns. Encourage students to distinguish attributes from entities. For example, a student’s name is usually an attribute, while student is the entity.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Identify Entities and Attributes
Scenario: A college wants to track students, courses, instructors, departments, and course enrollments.
Time: 8 minutes
Deliverable: A labeled list containing:

At least 3 entities
At least 2 attributes per entity


Give students 8 to 10 minutes. Walk around and check whether they are mixing up entities and attributes. Bring the class back by asking for one example entity and its attributes.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Relationships
A relationship describes how entities are connected.
Examples:

A student enrolls in a course
An instructor teaches a course
A department offers many courses
An order contains products


Explain that relationships are usually verbs or actions connecting nouns. Encourage students to write relationships as short sentences.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Cardinality
Cardinality describes how many records can participate in a relationship.
Common types:

One-to-one
One-to-many
Many-to-many


Introduce cardinality as the rules of participation. Use practical wording: one student can enroll in many courses; one course can have many students.

title: Data Modeling
Data Modeling
Data Modeling
text:
Many-to-Many Relationship
A many-to-many relationship means many records in Entity A can connect to many records in Entity B.
Example:

Many students can enroll in many courses
Many products can appear in many orders


Explain that many-to-many relationships cannot usually be implemented directly as two tables in a relational database. They need an associative table.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Draw Cardinality
For each statement, decide the cardinality:

A department has many instructors.
A student has one university ID card.
A student enrolls in many courses, and a course has many students.
A customer places many orders.

Then sketch a simple ER diagram for each. Label each relationship with a verb.

Give students 10 minutes. Encourage them to label relationships clearly. Afterward, review each statement and ask students how they knew the cardinality.

Keys in Relational Databases
Keys help identify records and connect tables.








Key type
Purpose
Example




Primary key
Uniquely identifies a row
student_id in Student

A verified, unique email address




Transition from diagrams to implementation. Explain that keys are what make relationships enforceable in a relational database.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Primary Keys
A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.
A good primary key should be:

Unique
Not missing
Stable over time
Simple to reference


Explain that primary keys prevent ambiguity. Mention that IDs are often used because names and emails can change or repeat.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Foreign Keys
A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key in another table.
Foreign keys are used to:

Connect related tables
Enforce valid relationships
Prevent orphan records


Use the phrase parent table and child table if helpful. Explain that a foreign key makes sure a course references a real department or an enrollment references a real student.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Find the Keys
Given these tables, identify the primary keys and foreign keys.
Student(student_id, first_name, last_name)
Course(course_id, course_name, department_id)
Enrollment(enrollment_id, student_id, course_id, enrolled_on)
Questions:

Which fields uniquely identify rows?
Which fields connect tables?
Which table resolves a many-to-many relationship?


Give students 8 minutes. Ask them to mark primary keys with PK and foreign keys with FK. Review that Enrollment connects Student and Course.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Composite Keys
A composite key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row.
Example:
Enrollment(student_id, course_id, term)
Together, these fields can identify one student’s enrollment in one course during one term.

Explain that composite keys are useful when no single field is enough. Also mention that some designers still add a separate enrollment_id for convenience.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Why Normalize Data?
Normalization stores each fact in the table where it belongs.








Problem
Example
Risk




Repeated data
A customer’s name appears on every order line
Updates can disagree


Insert anomaly
A product cannot be recorded until someone orders it
Valid facts cannot be stored


Delete anomaly
Deleting the final order removes the only product record
Valid facts disappear




Connect each anomaly to a business consequence. A normalized design reduces these risks by storing customer facts once, product facts once, and transactions separately.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Normal Forms at a Glance








Normal form
Requirement
Question to ask




1NF
Atomic values and no repeating groups
Does each cell contain one value?


2NF
1NF plus no partial dependencies
Does each non-key field depend on the whole key?


3NF
2NF plus no transitive dependencies
Does a non-key field depend on another non-key field?




Emphasize that normalization is cumulative. A table must satisfy 1NF before it can satisfy 2NF, and it must satisfy 2NF before it can satisfy 3NF.

title: Data Modeling
text:
First Normal Form
A table satisfies first normal form when:

Each cell contains one value
Each column describes one type of fact
Each row has a unique identifier
Repeating column groups do not appear

Order Dataset Normalization
An online store records customers, orders, products, and quantities.
Business rules

One customer can place many orders
One order can contain many products
A product can appear on many orders
Quantity describes one product on one order

Normalization Depends on Business Rules
The example assumes that:

Each product ID has one current price
One product appears at most once per order
Each order belongs to one customer

Different rules can require a different schema. For example, storing the sale price in Order_Items would preserve historical prices.

Functional dependencies come from business rules. Designers should confirm these assumptions with domain experts before finalizing the schema.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Key Takeaways

ER diagrams make entities and relationship rules visible
Primary keys identify rows, while foreign keys connect tables
1NF removes repeating groups and multi-value cells
2NF removes partial dependencies from composite keys
3NF removes dependencies between non-key fields
Row and key checks help confirm that normalization preserved the data


Close by connecting the three lesson sections. A strong database design starts with a model, makes relationships enforceable with keys, and stores each fact in the table determined by its key.

title: SQL Basics
text:
SQL Basics

SELECT: Choose your columns.
FROM: Choose your table.
WHERE: Filter individual rows.
GROUP BY: Bundle rows into categories.
HAVING: Filter the bundles/groups.
ORDER BY: Sort your final list.

title: SQL Basics
text:
The SELECT Statement
The SELECT statement is used to pick the columns you want to see.

Basic Syntax:
SELECT column1, column2
FROM table_name;
The Wildcard (Selects all columns):

SELECT * 
  FROM table_name;

The SELECT statement is the most common command. The asterisk is a wildcard, meaning “give me everything,” though it is often better practice to name columns specifically.

title: SQL Basics
text:
The DISTINCT Keyword
Sometimes a column contains many duplicate values. To see only unique values, use DISTINCT.

Syntax:
SELECT DISTINCT column_name 
FROM table_name;
Example:

SELECT DISTINCT country 
    FROM customers;

DISTINCT is incredibly useful for seeing the unique categories or values within a specific column, like a list of countries where your customers live.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 1
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

Display the FirstName, LastName, and Email of every customer.
Display each country represented in the Customer table only once.
Display the Name, Composer, and UnitPrice of every track.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Filtering with WHERE
The WHERE clause is used to filter records based on specific conditions.

It acts as a gatekeeper.
If a row doesn’t meet the condition, it is excluded from the results.

Example:
SELECT * 
    FROM products 
    WHERE price > 50;

The WHERE clause is our primary tool for filtering. It allows us to isolate exactly the rows we need from a massive dataset.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Comparison Operators
Use these to compare values in your WHERE clause:

= (Equal to)
!= (Not equal to)
> (Greater than)
< (Less than)
>= (Greater than or equal to)
<= (Less than or equal to)


These operators are the foundation of logical comparisons in SQL.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Logical Operators
You can combine multiple conditions using logic:

AND: Both conditions must be true.
OR: At least one condition must be true.
NOT: The condition must be false.

Example:
SELECT * 
    FROM users 
    WHERE age < 18 AND country = 'USA';

Logical operators allow for complex filtering. AND narrows your results, while OR expands them.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 2
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

Find the tracks that cost at least $1.00. Display Name and UnitPrice.
Find customers who live in either the USA or Canada. Display their name and country.
Find invoices from the USA with a total greater than $10.00.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Sorting with ORDER BY
The ORDER BY clause is used to sort the result set.

Default: Ascending (A-Z, 1-10).
ASC: Explicitly for Ascending.
DESC: Explicitly for Descending (Z-A, 10-1).

Example:
SELECT name, salary 
    FROM employees 
    ORDER BY salary DESC;

Ordering helps us make sense of data by presenting it in a meaningful sequence, like highest salary to lowest.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Sorting Multiple Columns
You can sort by more than one column.

SQL sorts by the first column listed.
If there is a “tie” in the first column, it uses the second column.

Example:
SELECT last_name, first_name 
    FROM employees 
    ORDER BY last_name ASC, first_name ASC;

Sorting by multiple columns is very common when dealing with data that has many duplicate values in the primary sorting column.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 3
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

List customers by Country, then by LastName, and then by FirstName, all in ascending order.
List tracks from highest to lowest UnitPrice. For tracks with the same price, sort by Name in ascending order.
List invoices from highest to lowest Total.


Ask students which column controls the primary sort and which columns break ties.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Aggregation: The Big Idea
Aggregation is the process of performing a calculation on a set of values to return a single value.

Instead of seeing 1,000 individual sales, we want to see the Total Sales.
Aggregation “collapses” rows into summary statistics.


Aggregation turns “row-level” data into “summary-level” data. This is where data becomes “information.”

title: SQL Basics
text:
Common Aggregate Functions

COUNT(): Returns the number of rows.
SUM(): Returns the total sum of a numeric column.
AVG(): Returns the average value.
MIN(): Returns the smallest value.
MAX(): Returns the largest value.


These are the heavy lifters of data analysis. COUNT and SUM are perhaps the most frequently used in business reporting.

title: SQL Basics
text:
The GROUP BY Clause
When using aggregate functions, we often want to see the summary per category.

GROUP BY tells the database how to bucket the data.

Example:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) 
    FROM employees 
    GROUP BY department;

If you use an aggregate function and a regular column together, you MUST use a GROUP BY clause on that regular column.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 4
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

Count the number of tracks in each GenreId.
For each BillingCountry, calculate the number of invoices and the total amount invoiced.
For each AlbumId, calculate the average track length in milliseconds.


Remind students that every selected column that is not inside an aggregate function must appear in the GROUP BY clause.

title: SQL Basics
text:
The HAVING Clause
WHERE cannot be used with aggregate functions. For that, we use HAVING.

WHERE: Filters rows before they are grouped.
HAVING: Filters groups after they are aggregated.

Example:
SELECT category, AVG(price) 
    FROM products 
    GROUP BY category 
    HAVING AVG(price) > 20;

This is a common point of confusion. If you want to filter based on a calculation like “Average” or “Sum,” you must use HAVING.

title: SQL Basics
text:
WHERE vs. HAVING








Feature
WHERE
HAVING




Usage
Filters Rows
Filters Groups


Timing
Before Grouping
After Grouping


Aggregates
Cannot use SUM(), AVG()
Used with SUM(), AVG()




A good rule of thumb: If it’s a simple column condition, use WHERE. If it’s a condition on a summary calculation, use HAVING.

title: SQL Basics
text:
SQL Order of Execution
SQL is not read from top to bottom by the database engine. It follows a specific internal order:

FROM (Pick the table)
WHERE (Filter the rows)
GROUP BY (Group the rows)
HAVING (Filter the groups)
SELECT (Pick columns)
ORDER BY (Sort results)


Understanding this is the “secret sauce” to debugging complex queries. If your code is failing, it’s likely because you’re trying to use a column in the WHERE clause that hasn’t been selected yet!

title: SQL Basics
text:
ACTIVITY 5
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

Find billing countries whose total invoiced amount is greater than $100.
Find genres that contain more than 100 tracks. Use GenreId to identify each genre.
Find billing countries whose average invoice total is greater than $6.00.


Have students first write each grouped query without HAVING, then add the condition that filters the aggregated results.

text:
Activity 5 Solutions
-- 1. Countries with more than $100 in invoice totals
SELECT BillingCountry, SUM(Total) AS TotalInvoiced
FROM Invoice
GROUP BY BillingCountry
HAVING SUM(Total) > 100;

-- 2. Genres with more than 100 tracks
SELECT GenreId, COUNT(*) AS TrackCount
FROM Track
GROUP BY GenreId
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;

FROM Invoice
GROUP BY BillingCountry
HAVING AVG(Total) > 6.00;

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
A common table expression (CTE) names a query result that you can reference within a single SQL statement.

Defined with WITH.
Reusable in the statement
Its scope ends when the statement ends.

A CTE helps organize query logic. It does not create a permanent table.

A CTE is a logical named result. SQLite can choose different execution strategies, so do not assume that every CTE stores a physical intermediate table. Source: https://www.sqlite.org/lang_with.html

title: Advanced SQL
section: The structure of an ordinary CTE

3    FROM Invoice
4    WHERE Total >= 20

6FROM large_invoices
7ORDER BY Total DESC, InvoiceId;

Read records from the Invoice table.

Read the filtered records from large_invoices.

text:
Joining a CTE to a table
Question: Which customers have spent the most?

1WITH customer_spending AS (
2    SELECT CustomerId, SUM(Total) AS total_spent
3    FROM Invoice
4    GROUP BY CustomerId
)
5SELECT c.FirstName || ' ' || c.LastName AS customer,
6       ROUND(s.total_spent, 2) AS total_spent
7FROM Customer AS c
8JOIN customer_spending AS s ON c.CustomerId = s.CustomerId
9ORDER BY s.total_spent DESC, c.CustomerId
10LIMIT 5;

Select each customer’s ID and add their invoice totals to calculate total spending.

9

10

The CTE summarizes invoices. The join adds customer names.

The output contains Helena Holý (49.62), Richard Cunningham (47.62), Luis Rojas (46.62), Ladislav Kovács (45.62), and Hugh O’Reilly (45.62), in that order after the CustomerId tie-breaker. text:
What is recursion?
Recursion is a process that uses its own previous result to produce the next result. It needs a starting point and a condition that stops it.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Parts of a recursive CTE







Part
Purpose




WITH RECURSIVE
Introduces the CTE definitions


Anchor query
Produces the starting rows


UNION ALL
Combines generated rows, keeping duplicates (Adds Rows to the new table)


Recursive member
References the CTE to generate more rows


Termination rule
Prevents further expansion when finished


Final query
Selects and orders the result



The anchor and recursive member must return the same number of columns in corresponding positions.

Use consistent meanings and compatible values in corresponding columns. SQLite’s flexible type system should not be treated as a reason to mix unrelated values. SQLite accepts recursive CTEs even without the RECURSIVE keyword, but this lesson includes it for clarity. Source: https://www.sqlite.org/lang_with.html

title: Advanced SQL
text:
First recursive example: counting
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
    SELECT 1                 -- Anchor Query
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1             -- Recursive member
    FROM numbers             
    WHERE n < 5              -- Stops expansion at 5
)
SELECT n
FROM numbers
ORDER BY n;
Result: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
numbers(n) explicitly names the CTE’s output column.

title: Advanced SQL
Advanced SQL
text:
All employees below Andrew

1WITH RECURSIVE team(EmployeeId, employee_name, depth) AS (
2    SELECT EmployeeId, FirstName || ' ' || LastName, 0
3    FROM Employee
4    WHERE EmployeeId = 1
5    UNION ALL
6    SELECT e.EmployeeId, e.FirstName || ' ' || e.LastName,
7           t.depth + 1
8    FROM Employee AS e
9    JOIN team AS t ON e.ReportsTo = t.EmployeeId
10)
11SELECT employee_name, depth
12FROM team
13WHERE depth > 0
14ORDER BY depth, employee_name;

1

Define a recursive common table expression named team with three columns: employee ID, employee name, and depth.

2

Begin the anchor query: select the starting employee’s ID, combine their first and last names using ||, and assign depth 0.

3

Read the starting employee’s information from the Employee table.

4

Choose employee 1—Andrew Adams in Chinook—as the starting point.

5

Combine the anchor row with rows generated by the recursive query, retaining duplicates.

6

Begin the recursive query: select each matching employee’s ID and full name.

7

Set the employee’s depth to their manager’s depth plus one.

8

Read employees from Employee, using e as a short alias.

9

Match employees to their managers in team. Each match finds a direct report; repeating this step finds employees farther down the hierarchy.

10

Close the definition of the recursive CTE.

11

Choose the employee name and depth for the final output.

12

Read from the completed team result.

13

Exclude the starting employee at depth 0, leaving only their descendants.

14

Sort by depth first, then alphabetically by employee name within each depth.



This query assumes Chinook’s acyclic hierarchy. The join follows a manager’s EmployeeId to employees whose ReportsTo matches it. Expansion stops when no matching reports remain. Later slides add protection for cyclic data.

Laura’s chain of managers

1WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
2    SELECT EmployeeId, FirstName, LastName, ReportsTo,
3           0 AS depth
4    FROM Employee WHERE EmployeeId = 8
5    UNION ALL

7           c.depth + 1
8    FROM Employee AS e

10)

12FROM chain
13WHERE depth > 0
14ORDER BY depth;

1

Define a recursive common table expression (CTE) named chain to trace an employee’s managers.

2

Begin the anchor query by selecting the starting employee’s ID, name, and direct manager’s ID (ReportsTo).

3

Assign the starting employee a depth of 0.

4

Choose employee 8 as the starting point.

5

Combine the starting row with rows produced by the recursive query, retaining duplicates.

6

Begin the recursive query by selecting the matched manager’s information, including their own manager’s ID.

7

Increase depth by one for each step up the management hierarchy.

8

Read potential managers from Employee, using the alias e.

9

Find the manager of the current person in chain: match the manager’s EmployeeId to that person’s ReportsTo. This moves up the hierarchy.

10

Close the CTE definition. Recursion stops when no further manager matches.

11

Combine each manager’s first and last names with a space, label the column manager, and include depth.

12

Read the accumulated rows from chain.

13

Exclude the starting employee, keeping only their managers.

14

Sort from the nearest manager (depth = 1) upward through the hierarchy.



Andrew’s ReportsTo is NULL, so the recursive join finds no next manager. Laura remains in the CTE at depth 0 but does not appear in the displayed result.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
Termination and depth limits
A recursive query ends when no unprocessed rows remain.
For these examples, expansion stops when:

A numeric condition fails, such as n < 5.
A join finds no more children or managers.
An explicit depth condition prevents another step.

title: Advanced SQL
text:
UNION ALL and UNION



Operator
Treatment of generated rows




UNION ALL
Keeps repeated rows


UNION
Discards duplicate complete rows




Duplicate elimination adds work. Select the operator based on the intended result and termination logic. Replacing UNION ALL with UNION does not automatically fix every cyclic traversal. Source: https://www.sqlite.org/lang_with.html

Pivot and unpivot in SQLite
SQLite has no built-in PIVOT or UNPIVOT operators.



Transformation
SQLite approach




Pivot
GROUP BY with SUM(CASE WHEN ... END)

An aggregate with FILTER (WHERE ...)


Unpivot
One SELECT per source column, combined with UNION ALL



A pivot query has a fixed set of output columns. New category values do not automatically create new columns.

       SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', InvoiceDate) = '01'
1                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS Jan_invoices,

FROM Invoice

COUNT(expression) counts non-NULL values. Without ELSE, nonmatches produce NULL.

Solution 4: why row counts can differ
The earlier long summary contains only country/year/month combinations with invoices.
The pivot contains every country/year found anywhere in Invoice. Unpivoting its three month columns generates three rows for each of those pairs.
Consequently, the unpivoted result can include explicit zero rows that were absent from the original summary.
The totals agree, but neither the row count nor the individual invoice detail must match. Unpivoting does not reverse aggregation.

JOIN Products AS p ON d.ProductID = p.ProductID

1              THEN ShipCountry ELSE 'Other' END AS country_group

                      THEN line_revenue ELSE 0 END), 2) AS USA,

                      THEN line_revenue ELSE 0 END), 2) AS Germany,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN country_group = 'Other'
2                      THEN line_revenue ELSE 0 END), 2) AS Other,

ORDER BY CategoryID;

Sum line revenue once into exactly one country column.

3

Keep the category identifier and label as row keys.

Independently rounded columns can differ slightly from a separately rounded total.
An order with three detail rows appears three times after the join. Summing its order-level Freight at that point would count freight three times.
Compute an order-level measure once per order, or define an explicit allocation to order lines before summarizing by category.
The inner joins include categories with matching order lines. Categories with no matching sales are absent.
